newsitem.title: USA: Space shuttle deploys U.S.-German satellite.
newsitem.headline: Space shuttle deploys U.S.-German satellite.

text.p: A small U.S.-German telescope was placed into orbit on Tuesday by the crew of space shuttle Columbia, eight hours into a 16-day science mission.

The Orfeus-Spas satellite was released from the mechanical grip of the shuttle's 50 ft.- (15 metre) long robot arm at 11:11 p.m. EST (0411 GMT) as Columbia soared over the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of Peru.
Shuttle skipper Ken Cockrell then fired manoeuvring jets to put a safe distance between the two craft. They will orbit about 60 miles (97 km) apart.
The deployment was one hour, 15 minutes late after pre-flight tests fell behind schedule, partly due to communications difficulties.

"The satellite (was) declared in good heath by ground controllers, their checks just taking a bit longer than anticipated," NASA spokesman James Hartsfield said from mission control in Houston, Texas.

The orbiting observatory's three-foot (1-metre) telescope will be trained on the interstellar gases that lie between the stars. This mysterious matter forms the building blocks of stars and is shed from stars as the die.

"By understanding these apparently arcane questions of interstellar gases we're learning a little bit about the eventual future of our very own solar system, as well as the general life cycle of birth and death in the galaxy," said Mark Hurwitz, one of the project scientists.
The Orfeus-Spas will fly free of Columbia for nearly two weeks before being picked up again by the shuttle's robot arm.

A second satellite, the saucer-like Wake Shield Facility, will be deployed from Columbia on Friday and retrieved three days later. The stainless steel spacecraft will use the vacuum of space to manufacture ultra-pure semi-conductors for the electronics industry.

Columbia blasted off from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre on Tuesday. The 16-day mission will feature a pair of spacewalks to practice construction techniques for NASA's planned international space station.
The crew of five includes Story Musgrave, who, at age 61, is the oldest person to orbit the Earth. NASA officials have told Musgrave his sixth venture into space will be his last.

The astronauts were not due back on Earth until Dec. 5 and will miss the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. They will, however, get NASA's version of the traditional family meal -- irradiated turkey is on the shuttle menu.
